# Beyond a fixed speed {#sec-extensions}

The elementary Lévy walk makes a strong modeling choice: a flight lasts a random time, but its speed is fixed. Real trajectories contain more information. A cell may choose a different speed after each turn; a perturbation in a fluid may broaden while it propagates; an atom may accelerate throughout an excursion. These mechanisms can produce similar mean squared displacements while producing different trajectories and probability densities.

This chapter develops the three classes of generalization discussed in Sec. III of @zaburdaev2015. The calculations also explain which parts of the elementary model survive a change of microscopic rules. Throughout, a renewal means an independent new choice of flight variables. It need not reverse the direction: two consecutive independently drawn velocities may have the same sign.

## A distribution of velocities

At each renewal draw a duration $\tau$ from $\psi$ and a velocity $V$ independently from a normalized density $h(V)$. During that flight the displacement is $V\tau$. The standard symmetric model is recovered with

$$
h(V)=\frac12\delta(V-v)+\frac12\delta(V+v).
$$ {#eq-ext-two-speed}

Let $\nu(x,t)$ be the density of renewal events, including $\delta(x)\delta(t)$ at the initial preparation. Counting completed flights gives

$$
\nu(x,t)=\delta(x)\delta(t)+
\int_0^t d\tau\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dV\,
\psi(\tau)h(V)\nu(x-V\tau,t-\tau).
$$ {#eq-ext-renewal}

To find a walker at time $t$, instead count its last renewal and require the subsequent flight to survive:

$$
P(x,t)=\int_0^t d\tau\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dV\,
\Psi(\tau)h(V)\nu(x-V\tau,t-\tau),
\qquad \Psi(\tau)=\int_\tau^\infty\psi(u)\,du.
$$ {#eq-ext-observation}

With the Fourier convention $\widehat f(k)=\int e^{ikx}f(x)dx$, a translated flight contributes $e^{ikV\tau}$. Consequently, the Laplace argument is $s-ikV$, and solving the renewal equation yields

$$
\widetilde P(k,s)=
\frac{\int h(V)\widetilde\Psi(s-ikV)\,dV}
{1-\int h(V)\widetilde\psi(s-ikV)\,dV}.
$$ {#eq-ext-general-transform}

This formula is exact for a fresh start at the origin. The numerator is as important as the denominator: it describes an unfinished flight at observation. Replacing it with $\widetilde\Psi(s)$ would describe a different process. At $k=0$, the identity $\widetilde\Psi(s)=[1-\widetilde\psi(s)]/s$ gives $\widetilde P(0,s)=1/s$, verifying conservation of probability. The random-velocity construction was developed by @zaburdaev2008random.

If $h$ is supported on $[-v_{\max},v_{\max}]$, every trajectory obeys $|X(t)|\leq v_{\max}t$. A Gaussian $h$ assigns a finite speed to each individual flight, but allows arbitrarily large speeds across the ensemble. There is then no common light cone. “Finite velocity during a flight” and “a uniform maximum propagation speed” are separate assumptions.

### An exact Cauchy example

A useful solvable case has

$$
h(V)=\frac{u}{\pi(V^2+u^2)},\qquad u>0.
$$ {#eq-ext-cauchy-velocity}

Condition on all flight lengths in time, including the unfinished last one: $a_1,\ldots,a_m\geq0$, with $\sum_j a_j=t$. Independence and the Cauchy characteristic function give

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{ikX(t)}\mid a_1,\ldots,a_m\right]
=\prod_{j=1}^{m}e^{-u|k|a_j}=e^{-u|k|t}.
$$ {#eq-ext-cauchy-proof}

The conditional result no longer contains the random partition. Averaging over that partition therefore changes nothing, and Fourier inversion gives

$$
P(x,t)=\frac{ut}{\pi[x^2+(ut)^2]}.
$$ {#eq-ext-cauchy-position}

This is exact for **every** duration distribution for which the renewal process is defined. Ballistic scaling here comes from stability of the velocity law, rather than from an infinite mean duration. Its variance and even $\mathbb E|X(t)|$ diverge, so an MSD exponent is not a meaningful characterization. The example is a warning against inferring microscopic dynamics from a single scaling collapse.

### Which tail controls spreading?

Suppose $\psi(\tau)\sim\gamma\tau_0^\gamma\tau^{-1-\gamma}$ and the symmetric velocity density has $h(V)\sim C|V|^{-1-\beta}$, with $\beta>0$. Integrating over one completed flight gives its displacement density

$$
g(\ell)=\int_0^\infty\frac{\psi(\tau)}{\tau}
h(\ell/\tau)\,d\tau.
$$ {#eq-ext-product-density}

The product $V\tau$ is heavy tailed because either factor can be large. Away from the equal-tail case, its tail index is $\min(\beta,\gamma)$: for example, if $\beta<\gamma$, then $\mathbb E\tau^\beta$ is finite and the velocity tail survives the integral with a finite amplitude. If $\gamma<\beta$, exchange the roles of duration and velocity. At $\beta=\gamma$, logarithmic factors generally appear.

This product argument must be combined with the renewal clock. When $\gamma>1$, the number of completed flights is approximately $t/\mu$, where $\mu=\mathbb E\tau$. Symmetric sums then suggest a typical width $t^H$ with

$$
H=\frac{1}{\min(2,\beta,\gamma)},\qquad \gamma>1.
$$ {#eq-ext-finite-mean-exponent}

Here $H$ refers to a typical spatial scale, not automatically to the exponent of every moment. When $0<\gamma<1$, the number of renewals is of order $t^\gamma$ and a few flights consume a finite fraction of the observation time. The resulting typical exponent, under these independent regularly varying assumptions, is

$$
H=\frac{\gamma}{\min(\beta,\gamma)}
=\max(1,\gamma/\beta),\qquad 0<\gamma<1.
$$ {#eq-ext-infinite-mean-exponent}

The marginal boundaries require logarithmic corrections. In particular, sufficiently heavy velocity tails allow superballistic spreading, $H>1$. Such behavior requires an unbounded speed law with divergent mean absolute speed; it is incompatible with a fixed maximum speed. Heavy-tailed velocities also make sufficiently high displacement moments infinite already at finite times. These facts limit the usefulness of moment-based phase diagrams.

For symmetric $h$ with a finite second moment and $\gamma>2$, a direct random-sum calculation gives ordinary diffusion. One flight has mean zero and variance $\mathbb E[V^2]\mathbb E[\tau^2]$. Dividing by the mean time per flight gives

$$
D_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\mathbb E[V^2]\mathbb E[\tau^2]}{2\mu}.
$$ {#eq-ext-random-speed-diffusion}

For $1<\gamma<2$ and sufficiently light velocity tails, the central stable profile retains index $\gamma$, but its scale contains $\mathbb E|V|^\gamma$. Its far tails retain more detailed information about $h$. This separation between a universal central shape and model-dependent rare trajectories will reappear in the infinite-density analysis.

## Fluctuations during a flight

Drawing a new velocity only at renewals leaves perfectly straight flight segments. A different model adds small fluctuations during a segment. Write

$$
dX(t)=V(t)\,dt+\sqrt{2D_x}\,dW(t),
$$ {#eq-ext-noisy-flight}

where $V(t)=\pm v$ is the renewal velocity, $W$ is an independent standard Wiener process, and $D_x$ has units of length squared per time. The white-noise term is a coarse-grained model for accumulated displacement fluctuations; it should not be interpreted as a bounded microscopic instantaneous velocity. This convention gives variance $2D_x\tau$ in a flight of age $\tau$. Some papers instead define a noise strength $D_v=2D_x$.

Integrating a single segment gives $\Delta X=V\tau+\eta$, where

$$
G(\eta,\tau)=\frac{\exp[-\eta^2/(4D_x\tau)]}{\sqrt{4\pi D_x\tau}}.
$$ {#eq-ext-noise-kernel}

Because independent Brownian increments add over the entire elapsed time, the complete process is exactly the elementary walk plus an independent Brownian displacement. Thus

$$
P_{D_x}(x,t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
P_0(y,t)G(x-y,t)\,dy,
\qquad
\widetilde P_{D_x}(k,s)=\widetilde P_0(k,s+D_xk^2).
$$ {#eq-ext-global-convolution}

In the superdiffusive regime the width of the central Lévy part is $t^{1/\gamma}$, larger asymptotically than the added Gaussian width $t^{1/2}$. The leading central scaling therefore survives. Near a ballistic front, however, the original singular peak broadens into a Gaussian hump:

$$
P_{\mathrm{no\ renewal}}(x,t)=\frac{\Psi(t)}2
\left[G(x-vt,t)+G(x+vt,t)\right].
$$ {#eq-ext-ballistic-humps}

For a fresh start, the total mass of these two humps is $\Psi(t)\sim\tau_0^\gamma t^{-\gamma}$. Their widths grow as $t^{1/2}$ and their heights decay as $t^{-\gamma-1/2}$. The equation identifies the contribution of trajectories without a renewal; other histories can contribute nearby, so the complete local profile need not consist solely of these humps at finite time.

For independent sign redraws, the full endpoint atoms before broadening have weight $W_{\mathrm{front}}(t)=\mathbb E[2^{-N(t)}]$, including renewals that choose the previous sign again. Their full Gaussian contribution is obtained by replacing $\Psi(t)$ with $W_{\mathrm{front}}(t)$ in @eq-ext-ballistic-humps. Since $W_{\mathrm{front}}(t)\sim2\Psi(t)$ for the power tail, the mass and height exponents are unchanged.

This gives an experimental discriminator. If a speed is drawn from a narrow distribution once and then held fixed, the displacement uncertainty of an unrenewed flight is $t\,\delta V$, growing linearly in time. Independent fluctuations accumulated during the flight instead give a square-root width. These two mechanisms and their front signatures are analyzed in @denisov2012fluctuations. Initial preparation changes the hump mass, a point developed in the next chapter.

## Identical renewal endpoints, different paths

A particularly instructive comparison keeps the same pairs $(\tau_i,\ell_i)$ with $\ell_i=\sigma_i v\tau_i$, $\sigma_i=\pm1$, but changes how each pair is traversed. Let $T_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau_i$ and $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_i$.

* A walk moves continuously from $(S_n,T_n)$ to $(S_{n+1},T_{n+1})$.
* A wait-first process stays at $S_n$ until $T_{n+1}$ and then jumps to $S_{n+1}$.
* A jump-first process jumps to $S_{n+1}$ at $T_n$ and waits there until $T_{n+1}$.

If $N(t)=\max\{n:T_n\leq t\}$, their positions are respectively

$$
\begin{aligned}
X_{\mathrm{walk}}(t)&=S_{N(t)}+\sigma_{N(t)+1}v[t-T_{N(t)}],\\
X_{\mathrm{wait}}(t)&=S_{N(t)},\\
X_{\mathrm{jump}}(t)&=S_{N(t)+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ext-three-interpolations}

All completed renewal endpoints coincide. Their current, unfinished segment differs, and for infinite-mean durations that segment is a macroscopic part of the history. Consequently, matching completed-step statistics does not determine the observed propagator. This distinction is central to the ballistic profiles studied by @froemberg2015ballistic.

For wait-first motion, the joint completed-step transform is

$$
\phi(k,s)=\tfrac12[\widetilde\psi(s-ikv)+\widetilde\psi(s+ikv)],
\qquad
\widetilde P_{\mathrm{wait}}(k,s)=\frac{\widetilde\Psi(s)}{1-\phi(k,s)}.
$$ {#eq-ext-wait-first}

The survival numerator contains no spatial shift because the walker waits at the previous endpoint. Every completed jump has a time cost already paid, so $|X_{\mathrm{wait}}(t)|\leq vt$. Conversely, the first jump in a jump-first process is made before paying its time cost. Its length is unbounded at arbitrarily small positive observation times; for $\gamma<2$ the MSD can diverge even though the continuously interpolated walk has finite moments. In the ballistic regime these models have the same exponent $H=1$ under the linear coupling but different scaling functions and different moment existence.

### Nonlinear couplings and a random diffusivity example

One may replace $|\ell|=v\tau$ by $|\ell|=c\tau^\eta$, with $c$ of units length/time$^\eta$. For an instantaneous-jump model this specifies the endpoint law. For a continuous path it does **not** yet specify the path: one must say whether the speed is $c\tau^{\eta-1}$ throughout a preselected flight, or whether motion accelerates with flight age. The last unfinished excursion depends on this choice. A nonlinear coupling generally removes the elementary model's uniform finite-speed bound.

Another useful coupling draws a Gaussian displacement conditional on the waiting time,

$$
\lambda(\ell\mid\tau)=\frac{e^{-\ell^2/(4D\tau)}}{\sqrt{4\pi D\tau}}.
$$ {#eq-ext-gaussian-coupling}

Then $\phi(k,s)=\widetilde\psi(s+Dk^2)$. For $0<\gamma<1$, the wait-first propagator has the scaling transform

$$
\widetilde P(k,s)\simeq\frac{s^{\gamma-1}}{(s+Dk^2)^\gamma}.
$$ {#eq-ext-fractional-diffusion-power}

This is a coupled space-time law: the denominator contains a fractional power of the entire diffusion operator. It is different from the uncoupled subdiffusive denominator $s^\gamma+D_\gamma k^2$. The general theory of such coupled limits is developed in @beckerkern2004coupled; a later correction clarifies technical assumptions in that theory [@meerschaert2012correction].

Finally, suppose travel over a distance $L$ takes $L/v$ and an added rest takes $aL$, with $a$ a time per length. The complete cycle costs $L(a+1/v)$, so its coarse-grained speed is

$$
v_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{v}{1+av}.
$$ {#eq-ext-effective-speed}

This elementary calculation explains why adding finite-speed travel to a coupled jump model changes even its apparent speed. A useful model must specify both its endpoint law and what occurs between endpoints.

## Exercises

### A front-width measurement

An experiment finds a hump centered at $vt$, of width proportional to $t^{1/2}$ and integrated weight proportional to $t^{-3/2}$. Under a fresh-start interpretation, infer the duration-tail index and the hump-height exponent.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The weight is the probability that the first flight has not ended. Hence $\Psi(t)\propto t^{-\gamma}$ gives $\gamma=3/2$. A normalized hump has height equal in scaling to its mass divided by its width, so the height is proportional to $t^{-3/2}/t^{1/2}=t^{-2}$. The width supports accumulated intraflight fluctuations. A distribution of fixed flight speeds would instead give width proportional to $t$ if its width is nonzero and time independent. The preparation must be checked before using the weight exponent.
:::

### Two diffusion constants

Take exponentially distributed flight durations of mean $\mu$ and symmetric independent velocities of variance $\sigma_V^2$. Compare the diffusion coefficient with the result when every duration equals $\mu$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
For exponential durations, $\mathbb E\tau^2=2\mu^2$, so @eq-ext-random-speed-diffusion gives $D=\sigma_V^2\mu$. For deterministic durations, $\mathbb E\tau^2=\mu^2$ and $D=\sigma_V^2\mu/2$. The mean renewal rate is identical, but a variance-weighted average gives more importance to long flights. Therefore the mean duration alone does not determine the transport coefficient.
:::
